issues.legal_issue: A materially false statement in an application to condone delay may itself justify rejecting the application.
material_facts: The acquiring beneficiary was a party to the compensation reference, appeared through counsel, and filed a written statement opposing enhancement.
The beneficiary stated in its condonation application that it was unaware of the position taken and the award, although the government had communicated its decision about the award to it.
The beneficiary took no timely steps to appeal after receiving that communication.
issues.conclusion: The incorrect statement was sufficient to reject the condonation application without further inquiry into whether the other averments showed sufficient cause.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, condonation depends on sufficient cause. A party should not obtain an advantage by taking a false stand to escape limitation; the Court relied on the decision reported at (1993) 1 SCC 572.

predicates.late_appeal_condonation_case: A party applied to excuse delay in filing an appeal.
predicates.applicant_made_false_awareness_claim: The applicant claimed not to know of a material decision or proceeding.
predicates.applicant_had_received_notice: The applicant had received communication showing that it knew of the material decision or proceeding.

issues.definition: When an appeal-delay applicant claims ignorance despite having received notice of the material decision, the application is rejected on the basis of that falsehood.

issues.legal_issue: A circumstance arising only after the limitation period expires cannot constitute sufficient cause for failing to appeal within time.
material_facts: The beneficiary knew of the award and the decision not to appeal before the limitation period expired.
It did not take steps to file an appeal before expiry and relied on later correspondence and requests to other authorities.
The appeal was filed after a delay of 1724 days.
issues.conclusion: The later correspondence and requests did not establish sufficient cause for the failure to appeal within the prescribed time.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 requires sufficient cause for not filing within the prescribed period. In Ajit Singh Thakur Singh v. State of Gujarat, (1981) 1 SCC 495, the Court held that the cause must arise before limitation expires and make timely filing impossible; a later event cannot constitute sufficient cause.

predicates.late_appeal_case: A party filed an appeal after the prescribed filing period had expired.
predicates.no_pre_expiry_obstacle: No circumstance arising before expiry made it impossible for the party to file the appeal in time.
predicates.delay_explanation_arose_after_expiry: The circumstances relied on to explain the delay arose only after the filing period had expired.

issues.definition: In a late appeal, where no pre-expiry obstacle prevented timely filing, later-arising circumstances do not establish sufficient cause.

issues.legal_issue: Negligence by a public authority or acquisition beneficiary is not excused merely because public money is involved, and settled rights should not be unsettled without a proper explanation for delay.
material_facts: The acquisition beneficiary knew of the award and the decision not to appeal but did not act within time.
After the limitation period, it corresponded with authorities and repeated requests that an appeal be filed, then filed its appeal years later.
The beneficiary relied on the involvement of public revenue, but no fraud or collusion affecting the decision not to appeal was pleaded and proved.
The landowners had executed the decree and received the deposited compensation.
issues.conclusion: The involvement of public money did not supply sufficient cause for the beneficiary’s prolonged inaction or justify condoning the inordinate delay.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to government authorities as it does to citizens, though relevant circumstances such as proved fraud or collusion may be considered. Under Ramlal v. Rewa Coalfields Ltd., AIR 1962 SC 361, sufficient cause is a condition precedent to discretionary condonation and diligence and bona fides are relevant. N. Balakrishnan v. M. Krishnamurthy, (1998) 7 SCC 123, explains that limitation serves public policy and does not license leisurely litigation. The Court also relied on the limitation-policy principles in Rajender Singh v. Santa Singh, (1973) 2 SCC 705, and Motichand v. Munshi, (1969) 2 SCR 824.

rule.if: public_acquisition_appeal_case and applicant_knew_of_award_before_deadline and applicant_delayed_through_its_own_inaction and no_proved_fraud_or_collusion

predicates.public_acquisition_appeal_case: The proceeding concerns a late appeal by an acquiring authority or acquisition beneficiary against a compensation award.
predicates.applicant_knew_of_award_before_deadline: The applicant knew of the award before the time to appeal expired.
predicates.applicant_delayed_through_its_own_inacti: The applicant failed to act promptly and relied on its own later correspondence or requests to others instead of filing an appeal.
predicates.no_proved_fraud_or_collusion: No fraud or collusion explaining the delay was pleaded and proved.

issues.definition: In a late compensation appeal, a knowledgeable applicant’s own prolonged inaction without proved fraud or collusion is not excused merely because public money is involved.

issues.legal_issue: A superior court may set aside an order condoning delay where the lower court condoned it despite the absence of sufficient cause and exercised its discretion on wrong principles.
material_facts: The High Court rejected the beneficiary’s claim that it was unaware of the award and of the government’s decision, noting that it had participated in the reference and had received the communication.
The beneficiary had not shown an acceptable explanation for its failure to appeal in time.
Despite those circumstances, the High Court condoned the delay of 1724 days.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s exercise of discretion was not judicial and could not be sustained; its order condoning delay was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 confers discretion to condone delay only where sufficient cause is shown. Although a superior court ordinarily does not interfere with a lower court’s exercise of discretion merely because of an error, an order condoning delay without sufficient cause, or on wrong principles, is vulnerable to correction. Ramlal v. Rewa Coalfields Ltd., AIR 1962 SC 361, confirms that proof of sufficient cause is a condition precedent to exercising that discretion.

predicates.delayed_appeal_condonation_case: A lower court considered an application to excuse delay in filing an appeal.
predicates.record_lacked_sufficient_cause: The facts and explanation offered did not show an acceptable cause for the failure to appeal in time.
predicates.lower_court_condoned_delay_anyway: The lower court allowed the application and excused the delay despite the absence of an acceptable cause.

issues.definition: When a lower court excuses delay in an appeal despite a record lacking sufficient cause, its condonation order is set aside.
